name: Gisaeng makeup and style imitation

card.summary: Copying the look of Joseon-era gisaeng, Korea's trained courtesan-entertainers, through hanbok silhouettes, hair and makeup for a period-inspired appearance.
card.note: A historical-costume style; specific makeup details are not well documented.

quick.overview:
Gisaeng (also spelled kisaeng) were women trained in the Goryeo and Joseon periods to entertain upper-class men with music, dance, poetry and conversation. Imitating their style means borrowing historical Korean dress, hair and makeup for a period-inspired look.
The visible payoff is a distinctive costume aesthetic. One documented fashion detail is the short jeogori (upper garment) worn with a waist band, which hanbok history says gisaeng started and which then spread to upper-class women.
quick.how: Enthusiasts draw on film and drama depictions and on hanbok styling, such as short jackets and fitted silhouettes, together with historical-style makeup and hair. Gisaeng paid for their own clothing and makeup, a detail noted in their history.
quick.risks: No health risks come from wearing costume or makeup beyond ordinary cosmetics precautions. Gisaeng were a hereditary low-status class, and their history includes servitude, which some readers consider when evaluating costume use.

lead: Gisaeng were women from outcast or enslaved families who were trained as courtesans to provide music, dance, poetry and conversation to upper-class men, in Goryeo (935 to 1394) and Joseon (1394 to 1897) Korea [1]. They paid for their own food, clothing and makeup [1].

Style imitation refers to modern people copying their appearance. Hanbok history records one concrete fashion link: women's jeogori shortened over the Joseon period, and the short jeogori with a heoritti was started by gisaeng and then spread to upper-class women [2].

Gisaeng appear in films such as Hwang Jin-yi and Chunhyang (2000) and Love, Lies (2016), which are visual references for modern styling [1]. Research on imitation of gisaeng makeup specifically has not been published.

chain: Borrow gisaeng-era hanbok shapes, hair and makeup
angle.text: The style changes appearance through clothing, hair and makeup. The short jeogori that gisaeng popularized is among its best-documented elements [2].

paras: Gisaeng belonged to the cheonmin, the lowest social class, and status was hereditary, so daughters of gisaeng usually became gisaeng too; they were nonetheless respected as educated artists [1]. They peaked at about 16 or 17 and were largely finished by 22 [1]. The Gabo Reform of 1895 nominally freed them, and in 1908 the Kisaeng Regulation Order placed them under Japanese police control [1].

Hanbok history under Joseon shows women's jeogori shortening from about 65 cm in the 16th century to as little as 14.5 cm in the 19th, with the short jacket worn with a waist band credited to gisaeng [2].
Films such as Hwang Jin-yi, Chunhyang and Love, Lies depict gisaeng, and the gisaeng training system has been compared to the K-pop trainee system for its discipline and performance preparation [1].
